title: Horizon-driven kernel activation and pulse flush controller for more stable streaming TTFB
author: Ava Martinez
body:
Context / motivation: Streaming-first-byte latency (TTFB) for short, interactive LLM sessions remains noisy under mixed workloads. Prior work improved emitter tick pacing and KV prefetching, but we still observe sporadic 100-300ms spikes when kernels are cold or competing microbatches collide. This PR introduces two complementary runtime mechanisms: (1) a horizon-driven kernel activation heuristic that proactively brings up kernel execution contexts based on a compact prefix horizon prediction, and (2) a pulse flush controller that shapes flush cadence as a function of outstanding credits, kernel activation state, and observed downstream ACK latency. Together these reduce tail TTFB without increasing steady-state token-cost.

What this change does (single continuous description): Implements a lightweight KernelHorizon predictor that consumes per-request prefix length, recent token issuance rate, and model-config microprofile to compute a short horizon window (in tokens) that is likely to be requested within the next emission cycle. The KernelManager uses the horizon to start kernel activation (allocate workspace, populate sparse KV slices, pin working set) ahead of inevitable demand. Activation uses a low-overhead fast-path that avoids heavy warmup if prediction confidence is low. The PulseFlushController coordinates flush decisions: instead of a fixed tick or credit drain, the controller emits a flush pulse when (a) the current emitter microbatch is above a dynamic urgency threshold, (b) kernel activation readiness crosses confidence threshold, or (c) a deadline slack indicates we must send partial output to meet SLO. The pulse controller also feeds back to the request-level credit allocator to temporarily increase credits for streams that triggered kernel activation, preventing self-inflicted head-of-line blocking. The feature is behind a runtime feature flag (runtime.streaming.horizon_activation=true) and gated by an experiment rollout that uses per-pod sampling and progressive ramp to 100%.

Engineering notes: The KernelHorizon predictor is intentionally conservative: it prefers under-predicting to avoid unnecessary memory pressure. It uses a short exponential moving average on inter-token intervals with model-config priors (max generation length, typical chunk sizes). Activation state machines are idempotent and cancelable; if the horizon estimate changes, activation can be deescalated to a low-power hold. PulseFlushController uses a leaky-bucket-style urgency accumulator with hysteresis to avoid oscillation under variable network ACKs. We record new metrics (runtime.kernel_horizon.confidence, runtime.kernel_activation.latency_ms, runtime.pulse_flush.count, runtime.pulse_flush.reason) and propagate them to tracing spans for waterfall analysis.

Performance summary: Bench results on q4-small (gpt-small-ish) workloads with mixed short chats and long completions: median TTFB improved 12%, p95 improved 18%, p99 improved 13% while token throughput remained within 1% loss. In microbench synthetic cold-start tests, the mean activation latency is 45ms (90ms 95th) with horizon pre-activation vs 170ms cold latency baseline. Cost impact: slight increase in transient memory allocations during activation windows (approx +2% GPU memory footprint on average for mixed workloads) but no measurable increase in per-token compute cost.

Compatibility & safety: Feature is disabled by default. Fallback behavior: if KernelManager cannot allocate activation resources within a short timeout, the pulse controller will revert to conservative flush cadence to prevent latency regressions. We added a kill-switch at pod-level to disable horizon activation in-flight. No API surface changes.

Testing: Unit tests for the KernelHorizon prediction logic and state machine, integration streaming tests that simulate varying ACK latencies and workload mixes, and an end-to-end perf harness run. Added deterministic replay tests to ensure activation cancellation doesn't leak resources. See tests/stream_perf_integration_test.py for scenarios.

Rollout plan: start with 5% of streaming pods for 48h, monitor runtime.kernel_activation.latency_ms and runtime.pulse_flush.count, then 25% for 24h, and full ramp if no regressions. Post-merge follow-ups include adding model-specific horion priors for large-context decoders and a telemetry dashboard to correlate activation events with p99 TTFB.

Related work: builds on ENG-3128 emitter pacing improvements and complements previous KV-prefetch PRs by focusing activation timing rather than cache policy. Also ties into Observability tagging work (ENG-3201) to surface activation events in traces.

review_comments:
Liam O'Connor: left nit on atomics in KernelManager::activate - prefer relaxed loads only where safe; confirm no ABA hazard.
Ava Martinez: replied - switched to seq_cst for the state transition edge and added comment explaining tradeoff.
Priya Raman: requested a safety test where activation fails under OOM and ensure no leaking; also asked for clearer metric naming.
Ava Martinez: added deterministic OOM simulation test and renamed runtime.kernel_activation.latency_ms to runtime.kernel_activation.activation_latency_ms for clarity.
Marcus Chen: approved after verifying integration test stability and that CI perf job shows no regression.
Pauline (SRE): asked to add a pod-level kill-switch; implemented and documented.
QA: found flakiness at very high ACK jitter - Ava added hysteresis and increased urgency decay window, re-ran tests.
Final: reviewers approved and requested squash merge.

merge: Merged via squash on 2024-11-29 by Liam O'Connor. Merge commit includes summary of KernelHorizon and PulseFlushController. Release notes entry added to docs/stream_tuning.md. Rollout configs added to runtime/flags/rollout.yaml. Merge strategy: squash and sign-off by reviewers.
release_notes: Improves streaming TTFB tail latency by proactively activating kernels and adaptive flush pulses; opt-in behind runtime.streaming.horizon_activation flag. See docs/stream_tuning.md for tuning guidance.
notes: Follow-ups: add model-specific horizon priors, dashboard for activation events, and explore combining horizon predictor with KV sampling policy for denser prefetch on high-confidence streams.
